title: Your first moves: three habits
outcomes: Takes space in the centre with a pawn on move one and says why the centre matters
Brings knights and bishops out toward the centre, one new piece at a time, and castles when the squares are clear
Knows these are habits with conditions: a threat or a concrete tactic can override them, and can name an example

steps.text: An **opening** is the first stretch of a game, roughly the first ten moves. Your pieces start boxed in behind the pawns, so most of them cannot move at all. The opening has one job: get your pieces out and your king safe before the fighting starts. The next board shows what is stuck at the start, and which single move frees two pieces.

steps.caption: Of the pieces, only the knights can move at the start. The bishops, queen and king are boxed in by their own pawns.

line.say: One pawn move opens a diagonal for the bishop on f1 and another for the queen on d1.
Black does the same on its side of the board.

steps.caption: After the centre pawn moves, the bishop on f1 reaches five squares and the queen on d1 reaches four.

line.say: The bishop jumps out to a long open diagonal and now looks toward Black's side.

steps.title: Centre pawn, edge pawn
steps.prompt: In the second case White opened with the edge pawn a4 instead of e4. Predict first: can the bishop on f1 move?

steps.text: The **centre** is the four middle squares: d4, e4, d5 and e5. Knights and bishops see the most squares from the middle (the next board shows a knight with eight against two). [I] That is why pawns and minor pieces are drawn there early. A pawn there also takes squares from the enemy and opens paths for your bishops and queen. That gives habit one: **start with a centre pawn**.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 reaches eight squares, the one on the h-file four, and the one in the corner two.

steps.text: What do the strongest players choose? Our own database holds 329,379 games between players rated 2500 or higher [V]. White's first move was e4 in 43% of them, d4 in 36%, Nf3 in 12% and c4 in 8%. The first two are centre pawns. [I] The other two fight for the centre from a distance, a second way to follow the same habit.

steps.caption: The d-pawn also opens a path, this time for the bishop on c1 and the queen on d1.

line.say: The bishop steps outside its own pawns to an active square instead of staying boxed in.

steps.text: To **develop** a piece means to bring it off its starting row to a square where it works. Habit two: bring out your knights and bishops, and bring out a new piece each time instead of moving one piece again and again. Capablanca (*Chess Fundamentals*) and Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*) both urged quick development, usually knights before bishops [S: our source sheets]. Treat it as a default.

steps.caption: Four moves, four pieces out. Each piece has a job.

line.say: The knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight too, and guards its pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black answers with the same idea and aims at f2.

steps.text: A **tempo** is one move of time. Count the moves, not just the pieces: if you spend two moves on one knight, your opponent has used the same two moves to bring out two pieces. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) treated development as teamwork, where the side ahead in it holds the initiative [S: our source sheet]. [I] Counting tempi is a rule of thumb, not a law: a second move is fine when it wins something or answers a threat. [H] Beginners notice lost tempi sooner when they count moves aloud.

steps.caption: Seven moves in. White has a knight, a bishop and a castled king working. Black has a pawn and one knight that went twice. Count the moves, not the pieces. [I] That gap is what players call losing time.

line.say: White opens with a centre pawn.
Black copies it.
A knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
A bishop comes out.
The same knight moves again. Black has used two moves on it.
White castles. Three pieces are working, against one for Black.

steps.title: Same knight, other square
steps.prompt: Both Nf3 and Nh3 bring the knight out. Predict first: do they work equally well?

steps.text: **Knights before bishops** is a common default, with a reason. [I] A knight's good squares, such as f3 and c3, are clear early whatever your opponent does. A bishop's best diagonal depends on where the pawns end up, so it often pays to wait and see. In the next board the bishop has several plausible squares, and one reply with a pawn changes the question at once.

steps.caption: White's bishop can go to b5, c4 or e2, and Black's pawns decide which is best. After the bishop goes to b5, one pawn move asks it a question straight away.

line.say: The bishop attacks the knight that guards e5.
A pawn asks the bishop what it wants to do. The pawns have changed the question.

steps.text: The queen is strong, so it is tempting to send it out early. [I] A queen out alone often gets chased by smaller pieces, and each chase can cost you a move. An early queen is not refuted by force, though: it works if Black ignores the threat. The next boards show the chase, and then what happens when Black does ignore it.

steps.caption: White's queen moved twice. Black developed two knights, and a pawn push gained a tempo by attacking the queen. [I] Black is simply ahead in development. Queen to h5 is not refuted: it works only if Black ignores the threat.

line.say: White opens.
Black copies.
The queen comes out and eyes e5 and f7.
Black guards e5 and develops.
The bishop joins the queen against f7.
A pawn attacks the queen with tempo.
The queen retreats and still eyes f7. White has used the queen twice.
The knight develops and shuts the queen's line to f7.

steps.caption: White's queen and bishop both aim at the pawn on f7. Black has just developed a knight and ignored them.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn, protected by the bishop. The king cannot capture it and has no square: checkmate.

steps.caption: Black to move. Several moves hold: attack the queen (g6), or add a guard to f7 (Qe7, Nh6, Qf6). [V] Checked at depth 16.

line.say: A pawn attacks the queen, so White must move it.
The queen retreats and still aims at f7.
Now the knight develops and blocks the queen's line to f7.

steps.text: Habit three: **castle**. Castling is one move that does two jobs: the king goes two squares toward a corner, behind its pawn shelter, and the rook leaves the corner for the middle. It is allowed only if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check and does not cross or land on an attacked square. Castling toward the queen is slower [I].

steps.caption: White's knight is out but the bishop is still on f1, between the king and the rook.

line.say: The bishop leaves, so one blocker between king and rook is gone.
Black develops a bishop too.

steps.caption: Both squares between king and rook are empty now.

line.say: The king hops two squares to the corner and the rook lands next to it, closer to the centre files.

steps.text: The king hides best behind its pawns, but every pawn move in front of it is permanent and can open lines for enemy pieces. Before the next board, see if you can find the fastest checkmate there is. It works only because White moved the two pawns in front of its own king.

steps.caption: After 1.f3 e5 2.g4, Black plays Qh4 and it is checkmate.

line.say: The queen slides along the long diagonal and gives check. No piece can block or capture, and the king has no square.

steps.text: A king left in the middle is a target. In the next board Black has one piece out, the king is still on e8, and a bishop sacrifice has dragged it onto e7. A castled king sits behind three pawns, as in the model game later, and enemy pieces have to get past them first.

steps.caption: Black's king never castled and its pieces are undeveloped. The knight from c3 delivers checkmate. This is a well-known trap, usually called the Legal trap [R].

line.say: Checkmate: the knight on d5 gives check, and the bishop on f7 and knight on e5 cover every square.

steps.text: The same three habits work for Black; the pawns just point the other way. Against a queen-pawn start Black can answer with a centre pawn of its own, then develop knight and bishop, then castle. Against the king-pawn start Black often fights for the centre from the side with a c-pawn, which is the same habit seen from a distance [I]. The next board follows one calm Black game.

steps.caption: One calm game from Black's side: a centre pawn, a pawn to support it, a knight, a bishop, and castling.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn answers White's centre pawn.
White offers a pawn to pull the d-pawn away.
Black supports the pawn and opens the bishop on f8.
White develops a knight.
A knight comes out and watches the centre.
White pins the knight against the queen.
Black develops the bishop and unpins.
White opens the bishop on f1.
Habit three: Black castles.

steps.text: A **threat** is a move your opponent could play next that wins material or gives checkmate. The three habits are for moments when nothing is threatened. When something is, deal with it first: capture the attacker, guard the target, move the target, or block the line. Here a threat appears in the middle of a normal opening.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop already aims at f7, which only the king guards.

line.say: The knight joins the attack. Now two White pieces aim at f7, and Black must respond.

steps.title: Same move, different moment
steps.prompt: Black wants to play the developing move Bc5 in both cases. Predict first: is it equally good each time?

steps.caption: If Black develops anyway, the knight takes the pawn on f7 and forks queen and rook. Black can win a pawn back with the bishop, but the position is difficult. [V] The engine calls it about -1.0 for Black at depth 16.

line.say: Black develops the bishop and ignores the threat.
The knight takes f7 and attacks the queen and the rook.
Black wins a pawn back with check, but the king and queen are both stuck.

steps.text: Habits have conditions. A piece that is attacked has to move, and moving a piece twice is fine when it saves the piece or keeps a strong diagonal. [I] The rule serves you; you do not serve the rule. The next boards follow one bishop that moves three times and loses nothing.

steps.caption: White's bishop has moved once. Black's pawn now asks it a question.

line.say: The bishop retreats but stays on the same diagonal.
The pawn attacks the bishop again.
The bishop retreats to a safe square on a diagonal that aims at f7.

steps.caption: The bishop has moved twice. [V] At depth 16 the engine's first choice is the retreat.

line.say: A third bishop move, but forced and useful: nothing is lost.

steps.text: Nimzowitsch, in *My System*, warned: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" [S: our source sheet, quotation checked]. He allowed one exception, a centre pawn taken without great danger [S]. [H] Beginners may lose more games by grabbing pawns than by forgetting to castle; our own game data could test that. Next time you play, count the moves you spend before castling and note any pawn you grab early.
Now watch all three habits work together in one calm game. Each step gives the reason, not only the move. Notice the order: a centre pawn, a knight, a bishop, a supporting pawn, then castling.

steps.caption: A quiet game of the Italian opening, move by move.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn takes space and frees the bishop and the queen.
Black copies the idea.
A knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black mirrors the move and aims at f2.
A modest pawn move supports the centre pawn and opens a path for the bishop on c1.
The second knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e4.
White castles: the king is safe in the corner and the rook is closer to the centre.
Black supports its centre pawn and opens the bishop on c8.
White gets ready to push the d-pawn, which would give it two centre pawns. [I]
Black castles too. Both kings are safe. White has one knight out and Black two; the knight on b1 still has to join. [I]

steps.caption: Black has two knights and a bishop out and has castled. White has one knight and a bishop out and has castled, so White is a move behind in development. [V] The depth-16 evaluation is about +0.2 for White.

steps.text: After castling comes tidying up. Bring the last pieces out, then connect the rooks, meaning nothing stands between them, and place a rook on a file that matters. [I] The castled king here sits behind three pawns. [V] The engine finds h3, Re1 and the knight to d2 equal. When several moves are equal, choose by plan, such as preparing a centre push. [H] Naming your plan aloud each move may build the habit faster.

steps.prompt: White to move. The knight on b1 and the rook on f1 have not joined the game yet. Before the questions, name the move you would play and the habit behind it.
Optional: play a short game as White from the start. Try to take the centre, develop a piece each move, and castle, and watch for the moment your opponent makes a threat.
Explain to a friend in three sentences why we start with a centre pawn, bring out a piece each move, and castle. Name one case where you would not.

steps.text: **One possible answer.** A centre pawn takes space and frees a bishop and the queen. A new piece each move gets the army working before the fighting starts, and castling tucks the king away while the rook joins in. I would skip a habit when something is threatened, such as a mate threat on f7, because answering the threat comes first.

steps.prompt: In the questions you just did, what did you check first: a threat against you, a piece to develop, or castling? Name the piece or square that decided it for you.
